16. It may be stated that on 28-3-87 the then President of Bangladesh made a declaration in the public meeting at Cheora that the Cheora Degree College would be taken as Government College. On 10-3-88 the Gazette notification was published vide notification dated 18-2-88 declaring the Cheora Degree College as Cheora Government College with effect from 19-9-87 and by that notification the Cheora Government College was nationalised. On 15-9-87 a deed of agreement was entered into in between the College Authority and the Government settling the terms and conditions of nationalisation including the retention of the teachers and other staff of the college as well as the assets and properties of the said college. In this deed of agreement vide Annexure-11 it is stipulated that: 

 17. Thereafter the Director General of Higher Secretary Education, Bangladesh, Dhaka, wrote a letter to the Principal of Cheora Government College on 17-6-87 stating that restriction was given for appointment of teachers and other staff of the aforesaid college from the date of declaration by the President, that is, 28,3,87. By this letter dated 17-6-87 the Director General, in fact, indicated that before the declaration of the President on 28-3-87 all the teachers and staff would be absorbed and the teachers and staff appointed after declaration dated 28-3-87 would not be absorbed. Annexure-K is the letter dated 15-10-87 written by the Director General Respondent No. 3 to the Secretary Respondent No. 1 requesting the Ministry to create 14 posts of teachers and staff including the posts of the present seven writ petitioners and thereby to absorb them. It is further stated that they all got the Govt. benefits. The petitioners got the salaries and remunerations as approved by the Government to a Government College teacher. Annexure-L contains the Rules which are called 'The Teachers and Non-Teaching Staff on Nationalised Colleges (Directorate of Public Instruction) Absorption Rules, 1981. In that Rules the definition of 'Teaching' is given under Rule 2(1) which runs as follows: 

 19. The petitioners tried their best for getting appropriate relief from the respondents, but the respondents did not give any reply to their representations. In such a situation they were compelled to institute a suit, namely, Title Suit No. 32 of 1992 for their absorption in the services of the aforesaid college. Annexure-(1) is the judgment of the Court which passed an order stating that the suit was not maintainable and the petitioners ought to have sought relief before the Administrative Tribunal. It is stated that since they had not been absorbed or accepted as Government teachers, they would not get any justice in the Administrative Tribunal or that their application would not be entertained by the Administrative Tribunal. 

 21. Now, the legal question arises in the instant cases in respect of all the petitioners that whether they are entitled to be absorbed in their respective posts in the aforesaid Cheora Government College with effect from the date of nationalisation of the College. Mr. MA Wahab Miah, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, submits that under law the respondents are bound to absorb the petitioners in their respecting posts in Cheora Government College which they held on 19-9-87, the date from which the nationalisation notification was given effect to. It is not disputed that in the notification dated 18-2-88 declaring the Cheora Degree College as Cheora Government Degree College was published in the Gazette notification on 10-3-88 and by that Gazette notification dated 10-3-88 Cheora Degree College was nationalised with effect from 19-9-87. Mr. Wahab submits that all the petitioners got their job in the aforesaid college much before 19-9-87 and since then they had been discharging their functions in their respective posts in that college. Mr. Wahab further submits that this Gazette notification of nationalisation of the Cheora Degree College as Cheora Government College, with effect from 19-9-87 should be read along with Annexure-D, the deed of agreement, executed in between the President of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, represented by the Upazila Nirbahi Officer and the College Authority, represented by the Principal of the Cheora Degree College. As we have quoted above the stipulation in this agreement is that the teachers and other staff working there in the college would always be treated and absorbed as Government teacher and staff by the Government. 

 22. In this connection we may consider this Annexure-I dated 17-6-87 which is the letter of the Director General of Secondary and Higher Secondary Education, Dhaka, which shows that the teachers and staff, in fact, would be absorbed who were there before the declaration by the President for taking up the college as Government college, that is, before 28-3-87. Mr. Wahab has challenged this order stating that this letter is dated 17-6-87 and the Director General was not authorised to give it a retrospective effect. He further submits that this letter of the Director General cannot override the Gazette notification vide Annexure-G published on 10-3-88 and the agreement executed in between the President of Bangladesh and the college authority on 15-9-87 for nationalisation of the college. It may be further mentioned that the self-same DG Respondent No. 3 issued a letter dated 10-10-87 requesting the respondent No. 1 for creating posts for absorption of the present petitioners and other staff in the said Cheora Government College. Mr. Wahab further submits that the petitioners were appointed in the services of the aforesaid Cheora Degree College before 15-9-87 and since they acquired vested right in their services before 15-9-87 and 19-9-87 on which date the college was nationalised, their vested rights cannot be taken away by the letter dated 17-6-87 which was, in fact, given a retrospective effect and this Director General had no authority to pass an order giving retrospective effect to the prejudice of the present petitioners who by that time acquired a vested right in their respective posts of the said college. Further, it appears that the present petitioners got their salaries and remunerations from the Government upto May, 1989 and it shows that the Gazette notification dated 10-3-88 giving effect from 19-9-87 and the agreement dated 15-9-87 had already been given effect to and in the eye of law the present petitioners were absorbed in their respective posts of the college by the Government upto May, 1989. Mr. Wahab submits that for giving salaries and remunerations to the petitioners by the Government upto May, 1989, in the eye of law, they had been absorbed to their respective posts and, as such, this letter of the Director General dated 17-6-87 cannot be given retrospective effect from 28-3-87. 

 23. We find substance in the above contentions of Mr. Wahab. By this letter dated 17 -6-87 the vested right of the petitioners cannot be taken away retrospectively in view of the fact that on and from 15-9-87 and 19-9-87 they had been absorbed as Government teachers in their respective posts of the aforesaid Govt college and such a vested right cannot be taken away by this letter dated 17-6-87 retrospectively. Mr. Wahab submits that even if this letter of the Director General is accepted, it may be accepted on and from 17-6-87, but not before that. He submits that a declaration may be given by any Governmental authority for nationalisation of a college, but it will be, in the eye of law, actually nationalised with effect from the date which is fixed by the Gazette notification in order to nationalise it. In the instant cases we find that although Gazette notification was published on 10-3-88, yet it was given effect from 19-9-87 and on that date, in the eye of law, the Cheora Degree College stood nationalised as Cheora Government Degree College and the teachers and staff who were serving there on the date, that is, 19-9-87, should be deemed to be Government teachers and staff of the said Govt. College. 

 24. In this case no affidavit-in-opposition has been filed on behalf of the respondents. Mr. Kaiseruddin Ahmed, the learned Deputy Attorney-General, appeared on behalf of the respondents and opposed these Rules stating that the Director General respondent No. 3 was competent to put embargo on the appointment of teachers and staff and since the Director General put embargo from the date of declaration by the President on 28-3-87, the teachers and staff appointed thereafter will not be absorbed. We have already discussed this point above and we find that there is no substance in the submission of the learned Deputy Attorney-General. 

 25. Mr. Wahab further submits that by Annexure-H dated 15-9-87, that is, the agreement between the Government and the College Authority, the Government promised to absorb the existing teachers and staff of the college when it will be nationalised and now the Government is not entitled to back out from its own promise which is written down in a registered document executed by the Government and the College Authority. In support of his contention Mr. Wahab has referred to the cases of Gujrat State Financial Corporation vs. M/s Lotus Hotels Pvt. Ltd. AIR 1983 (SC) 848; MP Sugar Mills vs. State of UP AIR 1979 (SC) 621 and 1981 BLD (AD) 91. In the aforesaid cases their Lordships have settled the principle of promissory estoppel. Once the Government authority makes a promise and in pursuance of such promise something is done, subsequently it cannot back out from its own promise and that is why they are debarred by the promissory estoppel. Mr. Wahab submits that since the Government made a promise in their registered deed Annexure-H to the writ petition and since the petitioners worked and got pay upto May, 1989, now the Government cannot back out from its own promise and they are bound to absorb the present petitioners in their respective posts of the college. We find substance in the above contentions of Mr. Wahab. The present cases are covered by the principle of promissory estoppel as settled by their Lordships in the above cases. 

 26. Mr. Wahab further submits that there is discrimination in the instant cases in view of the fact that teachers of Chaddyagram Government College which was also nationalised by the Government were absorbed in their respective posts and, as such, it offends Articles 27, 31 and 40 of the Constitution. He has drawn our attention to Annexure-P(1) to the petition which shows that one Mr. Abdul Momin Majumder was appointed as teacher of Chaddyagram College on 25-3-87, From a Gazette notification dated 3-3-88 it shows that this Chaddyagram College was nationalised by a notification dated 17-2-88 which was published in the Gazette dated 3-3-88 and this notification was given effect from 16-7-87, that means, though the Gazette notification was published on 3-3-88, yet the effect was given from 16-7-87 and as a result the Chaddyagram College was taken over as a nationalised Government College on 16-7-87. Mr. Md. Abdul Momin Majumder was appointed as teacher on 8-6-87 in that college. Annexure-P(2) shows that the Government absorbed him in his own post of the aforesaid Chaddyagram Government College with effect from 16th July, 1987, that is, from the date when it was nationalised by official Gazette notification. This Annexure-P(2) is dated 9-5-92. Mr. Wahab submits that similar question arose for absorption of the teachers of the aforesaid Chaddyagram College when it was nationalised. Ultimately this Annexure-P(2) shows that the Government absorbed Mr, Md. Abdul Momin Majumder in Chaddyagram Government College as a teacher with effect from 16th July, 1987. Mr. Wahab submits that similar is the case of the present petitioners and since the present petitioners were not given the similar and equal right, there is total discrimination in the instant cases and, as such, the respondents violated the provisions of Articles 27,31 and 40 of the Constitution. Article 27 speaks that all citizens are equal before law and are entitled to equal protection of law. Article 31 speaks that there will be equal right to the protection of law that means to enjoy the protection of the law, and to be treated in accordance with law, and only in accordance with law, is the inalienable right of every citizen, wherever he may be, and of every other person for the time being within Bangladesh, and in particular no action detrimental to the life, liberty, body, reputation or property of any person shall be taken except in accordance with law. Article 40 of the Constitution may also be attracted in the present cases of the petitioners. Considering the above it appears to us that the present action of the respondents, in fact, violated the provisions of Articles 27, 31 and 40 of the Constitution by doing discriminatory treatment between the teachers of one nationalised college and the teachers of another nationalised college though they are, in the eye of law, on the same footing. In support of his contention Mr. Wahab has referred to the case of Director General, NSI vs. Md. Sultan Ahmed, 1996 BLD (AD), 76. In this judgment their Lordships enunciated a principle to the effect that a double standard treatment meted out to different employees by the executive Government is deprecated. 

 27. Question may arise as to the fact that the salaries and remunerations of the petitioners were stopped from June, 1989, but why they filed the writ petitions in 1993. During this long gap what is the explanation of the petitioners given in their petitions. It appears that they worked in their respective posts in Cheora Government College upto May, 1989 with all the salaries and remunerations from the Government. When their salaries and remunerations were stopped, they made representations to the different authorities of the Government. But they did not get any relief whatsoever from them. Finding no other way the petitioners were advised to file a civil suit, namely, Title Suit No. 32 of 1992 for declaration of their absorption in their respective posts. But, ultimately, the suit was disposed of by a judgment dated 26-9-92 and the learned Judge in the ordering portion observed that the present suit is not maintainable and the petitioners should seek relief in the Administrative Tribunal. Mr. Wahab submits that since the petitioners were not treated as Government servants, the petitioners might not get the appropriate relief in the Administrative Tribunal. Further, he submits that since he has been invoking the fundamental right Nos. 27, 31 and 40 of the Constitution, the petitioners felt that the writ petition is the appropriate, speedy and efficacious remedy. Thereafter in 1993 they moved all these writ petitions and obtained the Rules. Mr. Wahab submits that after issuance of the Rule he tried his best to get these writ petitions heard and ultimately he is successful to get these writ petitions heard in this court. Explanation for delay given by Mr. Wahab appears to be reasonable. So, in our opinion, there is no inordinate delay in preferring these writ petitions in view of the fact that the Government did not give any reply at any point of time to their grievances so long and even before this Court the respondents did not appear with an affidavit- in-opposition denying the allegations or the claims of the petitioners made in these writ petitions. It appears from the aforesaid annexures that even in the year 1992 the Principal of the college wrote to the relevant authorities for absorption of the present petitioners to their respective posts, but without any result. 

 28. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case and the legal provisions as we have discussed above on merit as well as on the ground of fundamental rights as applicable in the instant cases, we are of the view that the petitioners are entitled to get relief in the instant cases as prayed for.
